special_tests.CSF_culture: Final report at 48 hours: Streptococcus suis isolated (alpha-hemolytic; identification by MALDI-TOF). Penicillin MIC 0.06 mg/L, susceptible. Ceftriaxone MIC 0.5 mg/L or less, susceptible. Vancomycin MIC 0.5 mg/L, susceptible.

contraindications: No known drug allergies; no contraindication to beta-lactams or dexamethasone.
interactions: Dexamethasone + Metformin: corticosteroids antagonize the glucose-lowering effect; monitor capillary glucose and use insulin as needed during the course.
Ceftriaxone, ampicillin + Metformin or Amlodipine: no clinically significant interaction.

warnings: Hyperglycemia (glucose 182 mg/dL) is likely to worsen on dexamethasone; frequent glucose monitoring.

Dexamethasone may blunt fever when judging response to treatment.
Vancomycin, if used: dose by levels and monitor renal function.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT attribute bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo to primary labyrinthitis and discharge the patient without lumbar puncture when fever and headache are co-present.
Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: the bilateral eighth cranial nerve deficit is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT delay empiric antibiotics awaiting culture speciation or MALDI-TOF results; empiric coverage must begin within 60 minutes of suspicion.
Do NOT omit adjunctive dexamethasone at the first antibiotic dose while the organism is unknown.

Do NOT interpret negative blood cultures as evidence against bacterial meningitis; bacteremia in S. suis meningitis is frequently transient and blood cultures are often negative despite positive CSF culture.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for bacterial meningitis.
required_recommendations: Draw two sets of blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose to preserve microbiological yield.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a cranial nerve deficit (bilateral eighth nerve deficit with severe sensorineural hearing loss) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified; for any other organism it can be stopped (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Reassess on identification of S. suis, since WHO 2025 permits discontinuation for pathogens other than S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae type b; any decision to complete the 4-day course for hearing protection is stated as a deliberate trade-off with its supporting evidence (in a Vietnamese randomised trial in which S. suis was the commonest confirmed organism, dexamethasone reduced death or disability in microbiologically confirmed bacterial meningitis; Mai et al., NEJM 2007; van Samkar et al., PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2015).
Recognise the occupational swine contact and raw-pork handling as the key epidemiological clue pointing to Streptococcus suis.

Recognise that bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction is the hallmark early complication of S. suis meningitis and must not be misattributed to primary labyrinthitis when fever and headache are present.
Note that standard multiplex PCR meningitis panels (e.g., FilmArray ME) do not include S. suis; definitive identification requires culture and MALDI-TOF or sequencing.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: penicillin-susceptible S. suis may be treated with penicillin G 4 million units IV every 4 hours or ceftriaxone alone, stopping ampicillin and any vancomycin.

Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation); with profound bilateral loss, refer early for cochlear implant assessment because post-meningitic cochlear ossification can preclude implantation.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical features of infective endocarditis (no heart murmur, no embolic phenomena, negative blood cultures, no sustained bacteremia); echocardiography is not part of the routine S. suis meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to the diagnosis or management of bacterial meningitis.
ECG has no role in the diagnosis or management of bacterial meningitis in this otherwise cardiac-healthy patient.
PET imaging has no role in acute pyogenic meningitis; CT and MRI cover all indicated imaging indications.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus suis

differential.key_features: Raised by the district clinic diagnosis and the bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with vestibular ataxia; excluded as the explanation by fever, meningism, drowsiness and a neutrophilic CSF (1240 cells, 91% neutrophils, glucose ratio 0.15) with Gram-positive cocci and S. suis on culture.
Clinically indistinguishable and also shows Gram-positive cocci in pairs; excluded by S. pneumoniae not detected on the multiplex PCR and S. suis identified by MALDI-TOF on CSF culture.

Diabetes is a risk factor, so empirical cover is given; against: cocci rather than bacilli on Gram stain, Listeria not detected on PCR, S. suis on culture.
Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, lower protein; excluded by marked neutrophilic CSF (91% neutrophils), glucose ratio 0.15, Gram-positive cocci and no viral panel target detected.

key_clinical_evidence: Streptococcus suis is an occupational zoonotic bacterium acquired from pigs and raw pork; pig farmers, abattoir workers, and raw-pork handlers in Southeast and East Asia are the principal risk group — the occupational swine-contact history is the key epidemiological clue.

Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction (vertigo, broad-based gait, positive Romberg) are the hallmark complications of S. suis meningitis, affecting about half of patients, and may appear early and dominate the presentation before classic meningeal signs are fully established.

The characteristic diagnostic pitfall in S. suis meningitis is misattribution of the bilateral hearing loss and dizziness to acute labyrinthitis (as occurred at the district clinic in this case) — the combination of occupational swine exposure, fever, and headache should mandate CSF analysis regardless of any prior ENT attribution.

CSF Gram stain showing Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains is consistent with streptococcal species; standard multiplex PCR panels do not include S. suis, and MALDI-TOF is required for definitive speciation.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified; for any other organism it can be stopped (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). For S. suis, completing the course to protect hearing is a deliberate trade-off (Mai et al., NEJM 2007; van Samkar et al., PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2015).
S. suis is typically penicillin- and ceftriaxone-susceptible; once susceptibilities are confirmed, de-escalation to penicillin G or ceftriaxone monotherapy is appropriate.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: In a febrile pig farmer, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction is the hallmark early presentation of S. suis meningitis; fever and headache mandate CSF analysis and the prior ENT attribution must be reconsidered.
red_herrings.data_point: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo presenting before meningismus is fully established, initially diagnosed as acute labyrinthitis at the district clinic
red_herrings.intended_effect: A naive agent may accept the prior labyrinthitis diagnosis and focus workup on ENT causes, deferring lumbar puncture and missing the underlying bacterial meningitis.
red_herrings.location: History of present illness (district clinic diagnosis of labyrinthitis)

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Bacteremia in S. suis meningitis is frequently transient; negative blood cultures do not exclude the diagnosis and the confirmatory test is CSF culture, not blood culture.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative blood cultures (both sets, no growth at 48 hours)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Negative blood cultures may falsely reassure the clinician or agent that there is no systemic bacterial infection, potentially leading to premature de-escalation or abandonment of the bacterial meningitis diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: a cranial nerve deficit (bilateral eighth nerve deficit with severe sensorineural hearing loss on examination). NICE NG240 1.4.7 agrees (new focal neurological features). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction present before full meningismus, creating a plausible primary ENT misdiagnosis (labyrinthitis) that an attentive agent must reject based on fever, occupational swine exposure, and progressive headache. Requires synthesis of occupational history, CSF findings (Gram-positive cocci requiring MALDI-TOF speciation, not in standard PCR panels), and understanding of the S. suis-specific hearing-loss complication and dexamethasone rationale.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required actions (labs, blood cultures, CT before LP, CSF), 1 recommended; 2 red herrings (labyrinthitis misdiagnosis + negative blood cultures); occupational exposure history is essential for organism identification; bilateral SNHL/vestibular syndrome as red herring creates moderate diagnostic challenge
metadata.real_seed_note: Seeded from: Petcharat C et al. 'Meningitis Caused by Streptococcus suis: Case Report and Review of the Literature.' PMC3325437, PMID 22523518, CC-BY-NC 3.0. The seed describes a 57-year-old male former pig farmer presenting with fever, headache, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with S. suis isolated from CSF; blood cultures were negative. The present case is a distinct fictional patient (56-year-old active pig farmer, Vietnam, different lab trajectory) inspired by this verified case. PMID verified on PubMed 2026-06-17.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Nguyen Van Minh is a 56-year-old right-handed Vietnamese pig farmer who presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, progressively worsening headache, neck stiffness, and bilateral hearing loss with dizziness. Three days ago he developed an abrupt onset of high fever (measured at 39.4 degrees Celsius at home), severe throbbing headache, chills, and nausea with one episode of vomiting. He initially attributed the illness to fatigue from farm work. The following morning he noticed he was unable to hear his wife calling him from the next room and described the sound in both ears as markedly muffled, as though his ears were stuffed with cotton. He also developed a feeling of swirling dizziness and became unsteady on his feet, needing to hold onto walls to walk. His wife took him to a local district clinic where the physician found the ear canals and tympanic membranes normal on otoscopy and attributed his hearing loss and dizziness to bilateral acute labyrinthitis or inner-ear viral infection. He was prescribed oral betahistine and sent home with instructions to rest. Despite this treatment, over the subsequent 24 hours his headache intensified substantially, his neck became increasingly stiff, and he developed photophobia. He also became progressively drowsy. His wife brought him to the regional hospital emergency department this morning. She reports he slept most of the journey and was difficult to rouse. He denies any prior ear infection, ear trauma, or noise exposure. He has no history of meningitis or encephalitis. Regarding occupational exposures: he routinely handles raw pork and pig carcasses without gloves when slaughtering animals on his farm; he slaughtered two pigs and prepared raw pork approximately 4 days before symptom onset. He does not recall any skin lacerations at the time but cannot be certain. He has not received meningococcal, pneumococcal, or any other relevant vaccination. His diabetes is reasonably controlled on oral medication. There is no known sick contact with meningitis.

neurological_exam.additional: Neck stiffness present with moderate resistance to passive flexion. Kernig sign positive bilaterally. Brudzinski sign positive. Photophobia noted — patient turns away from overhead fluorescent lighting. No skin rash or petechiae. No lymphadenopathy. Ear canals clear bilaterally with no discharge; tympanic membranes intact and without injection or perforation on otoscopy.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, briskly reactive to light. No papilledema on fundoscopy. No facial asymmetry. Gag reflex intact. Cranial nerve VIII: patient does not respond to finger rub or whispered voice bilaterally; examiner's normal conversational voice not perceived at 1 metre. Weber test: no lateralization of vibration to either ear when tuning fork applied to vertex. Rinne test not assessable reliably due to bilateral severe hearing loss. Remaining cranial nerves intact. No diplopia.
neurological_exam.gait: Unsteady broad-based gait on testing; veers and staggers without fixed directional preference. Romberg test positive — patient loses balance and requires support within 5 seconds of eye closure. Unable to perform tandem gait.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Glasgow Coma Scale 13 (E3 V4 M6). Patient is drowsy but arousable to voice. Oriented to person and place; confused about date. Speech is slow. Unable to hear examiner's normal conversational voice on either side; raised voice required for comprehension. Follows simple commands when shouted. Unable to cooperate with formal cognitive testing.
neurological_exam.motor: Full strength 5/5 in all four extremities. Normal tone. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Deep tendon reflexes 2+ and symmetric throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch and pinprick symmetrically in all extremities.
